exercises.title: Framing Effects
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in a behavioral economics class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Economists traditionally assumed that people evaluate choices mainly by comparing final outcomes. Behavioral research, however, shows that the way an outcome is described can influence decisions. Consider a medical treatment. If patients are told that ninety percent of people survive the procedure, they may react more positively than if they are told that ten percent die, even though the statistical information is identical. This phenomenon is known as a framing effect. Framing matters because people often use mental shortcuts when making complicated decisions. These shortcuts save time but can make logically equivalent options feel different. Importantly, framing effects do not imply that people are irrational in every situation. Experience, expertise, and careful deliberation can reduce their influence. Researchers therefore study not only whether framing occurs but also the circumstances under which individuals become less susceptible to it.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why medical statistics are usually inaccurate
How presentation can influence decisions
Why economists reject experimental research
How hospitals select medical procedures
questions.explanation: The talk defines framing effects: the description of an outcome changes decisions.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker compare two descriptions of a medical procedure?
options: To illustrate logically equivalent frames
To show that survival statistics are unreliable
To explain how doctors calculate risk
To criticize patients who avoid treatment
questions.explanation: Ninety percent survive and ten percent die convey identical information.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say about mental shortcuts?
options: They always produce irrational decisions
They simplify complex decisions but may introduce bias
They are used only by inexperienced people
They eliminate framing effects
questions.explanation: They save time but can make equivalent options feel different.

questions.stem: What will researchers most likely investigate in addition to the existence of framing?
options: Conditions that reduce the effect
The cost of medical treatment
The history of traditional economics
The number of available choices
questions.explanation: They study "the circumstances under which individuals become less susceptible".

exercises.title: Keystone Species
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today I want to introduce the idea of a keystone species. The term comes from architecture: the keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch, and if you remove it, the arch collapses. In ecology, a keystone species has an effect on its community that is far larger than you would expect from its abundance. The classic example is a sea star on the Pacific coast. When researchers removed it from an area of rocky shore, the mussels it normally ate spread rapidly and crowded out many other species. Within a few years, the number of species in that area had dropped by more than half. Now, notice what this does not mean. A keystone species isn't necessarily large, and it isn't necessarily a predator. Some plants and even some fungi play keystone roles. The point is the disproportion between how common the species is and how much the community depends on it. That's also why keystone species matter for conservation: protecting one well-chosen species can protect many others.

questions.stem: Why does the professor mention an arch?
options: To explain the origin of the term
To describe where sea stars live
To compare ecosystems to buildings in general
To show how mussels attach to rocks
questions.explanation: The term comes from architecture: remove the keystone and the arch collapses.

questions.stem: What happened when the sea star was removed?
options: The number of mussels decreased
Species diversity in the area fell sharply
Other predators replaced the sea star
The rocky shore was eroded
questions.explanation: Mussels crowded out other species; diversity dropped by more than half.

questions.stem: According to the professor, what defines a keystone species?
options: Its size compared with other species
Its role as a top predator
An impact much larger than its abundance would suggest
Its presence in coastal ecosystems
questions.explanation: "The point is the disproportion between how common the species is and how much the community depends on it."

questions.stem: What does the professor imply about conservation strategies?
options: They should focus only on predators
Targeting certain species can have wide benefits
They are ineffective on rocky shores
They should avoid protecting fungi
questions.explanation: "Protecting one well-chosen species can protect many others."

exercises.title: Oral Tradition and Memory
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in a literature class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: How did long epic poems survive for centuries before they were written down? For a long time, scholars assumed that performers simply memorized them word for word. But in the twentieth century, researchers who recorded traditional singers in the Balkans noticed something surprising. When the same singer performed the same story twice, the two versions were never identical. Lines changed, scenes expanded or shrank. Yet the singers insisted they were performing the song exactly as before. The explanation is that these performers didn't memorize a fixed text. They had mastered a large stock of formulas, ready-made phrases that fit the rhythm of the verse, along with typical scenes like an arrival or a battle. With these building blocks, they could recompose the story during each performance. This finding changed how scholars read ancient epics. Repeated phrases that once looked like lazy writing turned out to be traces of this compositional technique.

questions.stem: What did scholars originally believe about epic performers?
options: They improvised entirely new stories
They memorized the poems exactly
They read from written manuscripts
They worked in large groups
questions.explanation: Scholars assumed performers memorized poems word for word.

questions.stem: What did the researchers in the Balkans observe?
options: Singers refused to perform twice
Each performance of the same story differed
Singers used written notes
Audiences corrected the singers
questions.explanation: Two versions by the same singer were never identical.

questions.stem: What does the professor mean by "formulas"?
options: Mathematical rules for rhythm
Ready-made phrases that fit the verse
Written summaries of the plot
Rules that forbid changes
questions.explanation: He defines formulas as ready-made phrases fitting the rhythm.

questions.stem: What is the professor's view of repeated phrases in ancient epics?
options: They show the poets were careless
They are evidence of a composition method
They were added by later editors
They make the poems hard to understand
questions.explanation: They "turned out to be traces of this compositional technique", not lazy writing.

exercises.title: The Hawthorne Studies Revisited
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in a management class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: You've probably heard of the Hawthorne effect: the idea that people change their behavior simply because they know they're being observed. The name comes from a series of studies at a factory in the 1920s, where researchers varied the lighting and found that productivity rose almost regardless of what they changed. The standard interpretation was that the attention itself motivated workers. However, when economists later reexamined the original data, the story became much less tidy. Some of the improvements coincided with changes in the day of the week, and others with the replacement of two workers who were, shall we say, less enthusiastic. So the effect that gave the phenomenon its name is weaker than textbooks suggest. That doesn't mean observation has no influence. It clearly can. But it's a useful reminder that famous findings can rest on surprisingly thin evidence, and that you should always ask what the alternative explanations are.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the talk?
options: Lighting has a strong effect on productivity
A well-known finding is less solid than commonly believed
Factory workers in the 1920s were poorly managed
Observation never influences behavior
questions.explanation: Reanalysis shows the original Hawthorne evidence is weaker than textbooks claim.

questions.stem: Why does the professor mention the replacement of two workers?
options: To show that the factory treated workers unfairly
To present an alternative explanation for the productivity changes
To explain how the lighting was changed
To argue that attention motivates workers
questions.explanation: Productivity changes coincided with replacing unenthusiastic workers — a confound.

questions.stem: What does the professor imply by saying "shall we say, less enthusiastic"?
options: The workers were ill
The workers had not been productive
The workers were researchers
The workers had been promoted
questions.explanation: A polite understatement for workers who did not work hard.

questions.stem: What attitude does the professor encourage in students?
options: Acceptance of textbook conclusions
Skepticism and attention to alternative explanations
Distrust of all economic research
Focus on historical rather than modern studies
questions.explanation: "Always ask what the alternative explanations are."

exercises.title: Why Leaves Change Color
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Why do leaves turn yellow and orange in autumn? It's tempting to think the tree produces these colors as the weather cools, but for the most part, the colors were there all along. During the growing season, leaves are full of chlorophyll, the green pigment used in photosynthesis. Chlorophyll is so abundant that it hides the yellow and orange pigments that are also present. As days shorten, the tree stops producing chlorophyll and breaks down what remains, recovering valuable nutrients like nitrogen before the leaf falls. Once the green fades, the yellow and orange become visible. Red is different, though. Many trees actively produce red pigments in autumn. One hypothesis is that these pigments act like sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree is still recovering nutrients from it.

questions.stem: According to the professor, where do the yellow and orange colors come from?
options: They are produced when temperatures fall
They are present all season but hidden by chlorophyll
They result from damage caused by frost
They are absorbed from the soil
questions.explanation: The pigments are present all along but masked by abundant chlorophyll.

questions.stem: Why does the tree break down chlorophyll in autumn?
options: To produce red pigments
To recover nutrients before the leaf falls
To protect the leaf from sunlight
To increase photosynthesis
questions.explanation: It recovers valuable nutrients like nitrogen.

questions.stem: How is red different from yellow and orange?
options: It appears only in evergreen trees
It is newly produced in autumn
It is caused by chlorophyll
It appears in spring
questions.explanation: Many trees actively produce red pigments in autumn.

questions.stem: Why does the professor compare red pigments to sunscreen?
options: To explain a possible protective function
To argue that red leaves absorb more energy
To show that red leaves fall first
To describe how people use leaves
questions.explanation: The hypothesis is that red pigments protect the leaf during nutrient recovery.

exercises.title: The Bystander Effect
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in a social psychology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: In classic laboratory studies, participants who believed they were alone when someone seemed to need help responded quickly, whereas those who believed others were present often hesitated or did nothing. Researchers called this the bystander effect and proposed two mechanisms. One is diffusion of responsibility: when many people could act, each person feels less personally obliged to. The other is social influence. In an ambiguous situation, we look at how others react, and if everyone appears calm, we conclude that nothing is wrong. Now, here's a twist. A more recent analysis of real public conflicts, captured on security cameras in several countries, found that in about nine out of ten incidents, at least one bystander intervened. And the more bystanders there were, the more likely it was that someone helped. So the laboratory findings may describe what each individual tends to do, but in real groups, the presence of many people can still make help more likely overall.

questions.stem: What does "diffusion of responsibility" refer to?
options: Spreading information about an emergency
Each person feeling less obliged to act when others are present
Assigning tasks to group members
The tendency to look at others' reactions
questions.explanation: When many people could act, each feels less personally obliged.

questions.stem: How does social influence contribute to the bystander effect?
options: People copy others' calm reactions and decide nothing is wrong
People compete to be the first to help
People avoid situations involving strangers
People prefer to help friends
questions.explanation: In ambiguous situations, if everyone appears calm, we conclude nothing is wrong.

questions.stem: Why does the professor describe the analysis of security-camera footage?
options: To confirm the laboratory results exactly
To introduce evidence that complicates the original conclusion
To criticize the use of cameras in public
To show that people rarely help strangers
questions.explanation: Real-world data show frequent intervention, which complicates the lab findings.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the relationship between the two kinds of evidence?
options: One of them must be completely wrong
They may describe different levels: individual tendencies versus group outcomes
They both show that larger groups help less
They concern different types of emergencies only
questions.explanation: Lab findings describe individual tendencies; in real groups, more people still raises the chance that someone helps.

exercises.title: Dating with Tree Rings
exercises.context: Listen to part of a talk in an archaeology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's talk about dendrochronology, or tree-ring dating. Every year, a tree in a temperate climate adds a new ring, and the width of that ring depends on growing conditions. A wet year produces a wide ring; a dry year, a narrow one. Because all the trees in a region experience roughly the same weather, they share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings. Researchers have linked these patterns from living trees to older timbers, overlapping them like pieces of a puzzle, to build continuous sequences going back thousands of years. So if an archaeologist finds a wooden beam in an old building, they can match its ring pattern to the master sequence and identify the year the tree was cut, sometimes down to the season. The method has one important limitation, though. It tells you when the tree died, not when the wood was used. Builders sometimes reused old beams, so the date has to be interpreted with care.

questions.stem: Why do trees in the same region have similar ring patterns?
options: They are the same age
They experience similar weather
They belong to the same species
They are cut at the same time
questions.explanation: All trees in a region experience roughly the same weather.

questions.stem: Why does the professor compare overlapping sequences to puzzle pieces?
options: To explain how long sequences are assembled from shorter ones
To show that the method is a game
To suggest that the method is unreliable
To describe the shape of tree rings
questions.explanation: Patterns from living trees and older timbers are overlapped to build continuous sequences.

questions.stem: What limitation of the method does the professor mention?
options: It only works for very old wood
It shows when the tree was cut, not when the wood was used
It cannot be used in temperate climates
It requires the whole tree to be preserved
questions.explanation: It dates the death of the tree, and beams were sometimes reused.

questions.stem: What would the professor most likely advise an archaeologist who dates a reused beam?
options: Ignore the tree-ring date entirely
Treat the date as the earliest possible time the building was constructed
Assume the building is as old as the tree
Use only living trees for dating
questions.explanation: The building cannot be older than the cutting date, but may be younger — so the date must be interpreted carefully.
